query: For boride-based components used in hot-dip aluminum-plating equipment, what single intervention could improve resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion? Formulate one hypothesis that identifies the intervention, explains its mechanism, predicts the improvement relative to an appropriate baseline, defines the conditions under which it should remain effective, cites supporting prior evidence, and specifies a controlled experiment whose results could falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Pre-treating boride-based components with a surface aluminization step followed by controlled thermal oxidation will form a continuous, adherent alumina (Al₂O₃) scale, thereby improving resistance to molten-aluminum corrosion.
generation.material_initial_state: Boride-based components with a clean boride surface that may have low native aluminum content.
generation.intervention: First, perform a surface aluminization (e.g., via pack cementation or controlled chemical vapor deposition) to enrich the near-surface region with aluminum, then subject the component to a controlled thermal oxidation treatment in an oxygen-rich atmosphere.
generation.conditions: The pre-aluminization must yield an aluminum-enriched layer (~a few hundred nanometers thick) followed by oxidation at temperatures between 450–600 °C under controlled oxygen partial pressure to form a thin, dense, and adherent alumina scale; subsequent exposure to molten aluminum occurs under standard hot-dip conditions.
generation.structural_mediator: The combined pre-aluminization and oxidation treatment creates a uniform alumina scale that is well-bonded to the underlying, aluminum-enriched boride matrix.
generation.mechanism: The protective alumina scale serves as an effective diffusion barrier that prevents molten aluminum from reacting with the substrate, thereby reducing corrosion by limiting infiltration and dissolution processes.
generation.predicted_outcome: Pre-treated samples will display a significantly lower corrosion rate (evidenced by lower mass loss and reduced oxide spallation) compared to untreated samples when exposed to molten aluminum.
generation.baseline: Boride-based components without any surface treatment, which are more prone to aggressive molten-aluminum attack.
generation.boundary: The success of this approach hinges on achieving a uniform, defect-free alumina scale; if the pre-treated layer is too thick or poorly adherent, it may spall under plating conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact improvement in corrosion resistance and the long-term stability of the alumina scale under repeated thermal cycling need to be empirically validated.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of samples: one set receiving the pre-aluminization plus controlled oxidation treatment and one untreated control set. Expose both to identical molten aluminum hot-dip plating conditions.
measurements: SEM/EDS imaging to evaluate the integrity and continuity of the alumina scale
XRD analysis to confirm the formation and phase purity of the alumina layer
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated samples do not exhibit a statistically significant reduction in corrosion damage (mass loss, spallation, or interfacial degradation) compared to untreated samples, or if the alumina scale fails under thermal cycling, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: The oxide scale morphologies of the coatings are shown in Figure 10c,g and the EDS analysis is shown in Table 4. It can be concluded that the oxidation corrosion products of the coatings were mainly Al-rich oxides. Additionally, there was also a certain amount of FeCr-rich oxides. Combined with the XRD results in Figure 9, it can be concluded that the corrosion product was mainly Al2O3. By analyzing the morphology and EDS of the corroded areas, it can be concluded that the elemental depletion of the EHEA coating was faster than that of the YHf coating, and trace amounts of sulfur elements were detected in the corroded areas of the EHEA. In conclusion, all coatings exhibited the same corrosion mechanism. The YHf-EHEA coating showed better resistance to the 75% Na2SO4 + 25% NaCl molten salts hot corrosion than the EHEA coating at 900 °C. The mechanism for the coatings under Na2SO4 + NaCl hot corrosion is described as follows [,,,]. Initially, chlorine reacts with the metal to form metal chlorides (MClx). However, at a temperature of 900 °C, the metal oxides (MxOy) have a lower Gibbs formation free energy than the metal chlorides, leading to the transformation of the metal chlorides i

Corrosion resistance of alloys in light water reactors (LWRs) and more generally in oxidative environments is achieved by the formation of protective oxide layers that hinder further oxidation. Alloys containing Cr, Al, or Si typically tend to form a compact and self-healing chromia (Cr2O3), alumina (Al2O3) or silica (SiO2) layers, respectively, which acts as effective diffusion barriers against further oxidation. However, in molten fluoride salts (salt of choice for many molten salt reactor concepts, MSRs) these protective oxide layers on structural alloys are unstable which in turn leads to the dissolution of the least noble element in the alloy. Such a corrosion mechanism can lead to a reduction in components’ wall thickness and eventually the loss of the structural integrity of the reactor components,. The dissolution products themselves may lead to plate-out in the relatively cooler sections of the system due to the strong sensitivity of solubility of analytes to temperature.
